doc.title: Objects and Arrays
doc.paragraph: Adaptive Script uses two main structured values: object (named properties) and array (ordered sequence of values). Operations on them are Adaptive Functions registered in the environment, not methods attached to type objects or inherited through a type hierarchy. Many of those functions may also be called with method-style sugar when marked as data-type methods: value->function(…) (the receiver is the first parameter).

Per-function signatures and details are generated under the Function Reference (categories object, array, higher_order_array, and polymorphic methods such as freeze and length). This page is a language-oriented overview of everyday object and array work, including helpers added for issue #55.

Object values use property names and values. A property name may be an identifier, a string literal, or an expression in square brackets. Bracket expressions are evaluated when the object value is evaluated; the result is the property name (a string). Names that are not valid identifiers (for example names with spaces) use a string literal or a bracket expression. The same bracket form is used for obj[name] get and assignment on an existing object.

Core property helpers include property_get, property_exists, property_delete, and add_properties. Prefer property_get(obj, name, default) when a missing property should supply a default; built-ins that return a default clone mutable defaults so callers do not share a single permanent empty object or array.

Each call builds a new array (a snapshot of names, values, or pairs at that moment). Later changes to the object do not update an earlier snapshot. Order follows the object’s property iteration order.
entries returns an array of two-element arrays [name, value]. That is convenient for for-of and higher-order functions such as map / filter.

doc.paragraph: Arrays are ordered sequences. Literals use square brackets. Indexing is zero-based. In normal script use, arrays are dense sequences of values (every index from zero through length minus one holds an entry).

length (and the bag-oriented bag_size) return the number of entries. slice, join, reverse, sort, and higher-order functions such as map, filter, find, and reduce are ordinary Adaptive functions that take arrays as arguments (or as the receiver when used as data-type methods).

section.paragraph: at(array, index) returns the value at a signed index. Negative indexes count from the end (-1 is the last element). Out of range yields undefined (nullish), not an error.
These functions require a mutable array (not frozen). They modify the target in place.
push / pop form a stack (LIFO). push / shift form a queue (FIFO). Method form is available, for example a->push(4), a->pop().

splice(array, startIndex, deleteCount?, …values) removes zero or more values starting at startIndex and optionally inserts new values there. It returns an array of the removed values. Negative startIndex counts from the end. If deleteCount is omitted, all values from the start index through the end are removed.
freeze(value) makes an object or array immutable so further mutation throws. Freezing an already immutable value is a no-op. The same value is returned.
Script object and array literals used as defaults or shared values may already be immutable in some contexts. Prefer clone when you need an independent mutable copy.

section.header: Testing every element or any element
section.paragraph: every(predicate, array, …) and some(predicate, array, …) return whether all or any values pass a boolean predicate. They share the same implementation family as all_of and any_of (including multi-array forms). An empty array yields true for every and false for some.
Use all_of / any_of when you already rely on that naming or need the wider quantifier family documented under higher-order array functions.

doc.paragraph: for (let x of array) walks array values in order. Objects are not for-of iterable as a whole; iterate keys, values, or entries instead.

Function Reference categories: object, array, higher_order_array, and polymorphic methods (length, clone, freeze, and others). See also Language Features and Qualified Variables for additional language and host-context material.
